title: Diagnostic Ultrasonography
description: Ultrasound physics and instrumentation, Doppler, artefacts, and obstetric, abdominal, pelvic and point-of-care applications.

topics.title: Ultrasound Physics and Transducers
topics.summary: Sound propagation, acoustic impedance, reflection, attenuation and transducer types.

notes.b: Diagnostic ultrasound uses sound above 20 kHz (typically 2–15 MHz), generated and received by piezoelectric crystals in the transducer (pulse–echo principle). The average speed of sound in soft tissue is 1,540 m/s, which scanners assume to calculate depth (depth = speed × time ÷ 2). Acoustic impedance (Z = density × speed) differences at tissue interfaces determine reflection: large differences (soft tissue–air, soft tissue–bone) reflect almost all sound, which is why coupling gel is needed and why gas-filled bowel and bone limit imaging. Attenuation (absorption, scattering, reflection) increases with frequency and depth — high frequencies give better axial resolution but less penetration.
k: Higher frequency: better resolution, less penetration

notes.b: Transducer types: linear array (high frequency, rectangular image — superficial structures, vessels, musculoskeletal, thyroid, breast), curvilinear/convex (lower frequency, wide field — abdomen and obstetrics), phased array (small footprint, sector image — cardiac, intercostal) and endocavitary (transvaginal, transrectal — high frequency close to organs). Axial resolution depends on spatial pulse length (improved by higher frequency); lateral resolution depends on beam width (best at the focal zone). Controls: overall gain, time-gain compensation (TGC — compensates for attenuation with depth), depth, focus position and frequency. The ALARA principle applies: minimise exposure time and output (thermal and mechanical indices).
k: Linear: superficial; curvilinear: abdomen; phased: cardiac

topics.title: Doppler and Artefacts
topics.summary: Doppler principle, colour and spectral Doppler, aliasing, and common imaging artefacts.

notes.b: The Doppler effect is the change in frequency of sound reflected from moving targets (red blood cells): Δf = 2f0v cos θ / c. The insonation angle should be less than 60° for accurate velocity measurement (cos 90° = 0, so no Doppler signal at 90°). Modes: colour Doppler (direction and mean velocity mapped as colour — by convention red towards and blue away from the transducer: 'BART'), power Doppler (sensitive to slow flow, no direction), and spectral (pulsed-wave) Doppler (velocity waveform at a sample volume — measures peak systolic velocity, resistance and pulsatility indices; used in umbilical artery, carotid, renal and transcranial studies). Continuous-wave Doppler measures high velocities without aliasing but cannot localise depth.

Aliasing occurs in pulsed Doppler when the Doppler shift exceeds the Nyquist limit (half the pulse repetition frequency), causing wrap-around of the waveform or colour — correct by increasing PRF/scale, lowering transducer frequency, moving the baseline or increasing the angle. Grey-scale artefacts: acoustic shadowing (behind gallstones, kidney stones, bone — diagnostically useful), posterior acoustic enhancement (behind fluid-filled cysts — confirms fluid), reverberation (multiple equally spaced lines between two strong reflectors; comet-tail artefacts), mirror image (e.g. liver appearing above the diaphragm), refraction (edge shadows) and side-lobe artefacts. Recognising artefacts prevents misdiagnosis and some (shadowing, enhancement) aid diagnosis.
k: Aliasing: exceed Nyquist limit — raise PRF

topics.title: Obstetric Ultrasound
topics.summary: Early pregnancy, dating and biometry, anomaly scanning, placenta and liquor, and fetal well-being.

notes.b: Transvaginal ultrasound detects an intrauterine gestational sac at about 4.5–5 weeks; the yolk sac appears at about 5–5.5 weeks and the embryo with cardiac activity at about 6 weeks. An empty uterus with a positive pregnancy test raises concern for ectopic pregnancy (look for adnexal mass and free fluid). Crown–rump length (CRL) between 7 and 14 weeks is the most accurate method of dating. After 14 weeks, biometry uses biparietal diameter (BPD), head circumference (HC), abdominal circumference (AC) and femur length (FL) to estimate gestational age and fetal weight; AC is most sensitive to growth restriction. First-trimester nuchal translucency (11–14 weeks) screens for chromosomal abnormalities.
k: Empty uterus + positive test → exclude ectopic

notes.b: The mid-trimester anomaly scan (18–22 weeks) examines fetal anatomy (neural tube, heart, abdominal wall, kidneys, limbs, face). Placental localisation: a low-lying placenta or placenta praevia (covering the internal os) found at the anomaly scan is rechecked at about 32 weeks; placenta accreta spectrum is suspected after previous caesarean sections. Amniotic fluid: assessed by the deepest vertical pocket or amniotic fluid index (AFI — normal about 5–25 cm); oligohydramnios (renal agenesis, growth restriction, rupture of membranes) and polyhydramnios (diabetes, fetal GI atresia, anencephaly). Growth assessment and umbilical artery Doppler (absent or reversed end-diastolic flow indicates severe placental insufficiency) monitor high-risk pregnancies; the biophysical profile assesses fetal well-being. Multiple pregnancy chorionicity is best determined in the first trimester (lambda vs T sign).

topics.title: Abdominal and Pelvic Ultrasound
topics.summary: Liver, gallbladder, kidneys, spleen, pelvis and common pathology.

notes.b: The patient fasts for about 6 hours before upper abdominal ultrasound to distend the gallbladder and reduce bowel gas. Liver: size, echotexture (fatty liver — bright/echogenic; cirrhosis — coarse, nodular surface, ascites, splenomegaly), focal lesions (hepatocellular carcinoma — common with hepatitis B; amoebic abscess — hypoechoic lesion; hydatid cyst). Gallbladder: gallstones (echogenic, shadowing, mobile), cholecystitis (wall thickening > 3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign); common bile duct dilatation (> 6 mm) suggests obstruction. Kidneys: normal adult length about 10–12 cm; hydronephrosis (dilated pelvicalyceal system), stones, cysts (polycystic kidney disease), small echogenic kidneys in chronic kidney disease. Spleen: splenomegaly (> 12–13 cm) in malaria, sickle cell (early), portal hypertension and haematological disease. Schistosomiasis causes periportal fibrosis visible as echogenic bands.
k: Fast 6 hours before upper abdominal scan
Kidney 10–12 cm; small echogenic in CKD

notes.b: Transabdominal pelvic scanning requires a full bladder as an acoustic window; transvaginal scanning (empty bladder) gives better detail of the uterus and ovaries. Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas — very common in Nigerian women) appear as well-defined hypoechoic masses; ovarian cysts (simple anechoic vs complex); pelvic inflammatory disease and tubo-ovarian abscess; endometrial thickness in postmenopausal bleeding (> 4 mm warrants evaluation). Prostate volume in men with urinary symptoms and post-void residual volume. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS): FAST/eFAST in trauma (free fluid in Morison's pouch, splenorenal recess, pelvis and pericardium; pneumothorax), guidance for procedures (IV access, effusion drainage), and assessment of pregnancy, heart and lungs — increasingly used in Nigerian emergency and primary care settings.
k: Full bladder for transabdominal pelvic scan
FAST: Morison's pouch, splenorenal, pelvis, pericardium

topics.title: Vascular, Small Parts and Musculoskeletal Ultrasound
topics.summary: Carotid and venous Doppler, thyroid, breast, scrotal and musculoskeletal applications.

notes.b: Deep vein thrombosis is diagnosed with compression ultrasound: a normal vein collapses completely with probe pressure; a thrombosed vein is non-compressible and may contain echogenic thrombus, with absent flow. Carotid Doppler grades internal carotid stenosis using peak systolic velocity and plaque appearance (important in stroke prevention). Renal artery Doppler and arterial studies of the limbs (peripheral arterial disease) are other applications; arteriovenous fistula assessment supports haemodialysis. Echocardiography evaluates cardiac function, valves (rheumatic heart disease screening in schools), pericardial effusion and congenital heart disease.

Thyroid ultrasound characterises nodules (features suggesting malignancy: hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, irregular margins, taller-than-wide shape) and guides fine-needle aspiration (TIRADS scoring). Breast ultrasound is the first-line imaging in young women (dense breasts) and characterises lumps seen on mammography (simple cyst vs solid mass; BI-RADS). Scrotal ultrasound evaluates testicular torsion (absent flow — surgical emergency), epididymo-orchitis (increased flow), hydrocoele and testicular tumours. Musculoskeletal ultrasound assesses tendons (tears, tendinopathy), joint effusions, soft-tissue masses and abscesses, and guides injections. In infants, ultrasound assesses developmental dysplasia of the hip (Graf method) and pyloric stenosis (muscle thickness > 3 mm, length > 15 mm).
